nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How has apitherapy tourism developed in relation to beekeeping in Europe?
nodes.answer: Apitherapy tourism has emerged as a new economic branch, influenced by market demand, advancements in beekeeping technology, and new knowledge about the health-giving properties of beekeeping products.
nodes.paragraph: Due to the increasing market demand for health-promoting products, beekeepers have started to enhance their products by mixing beekeeping products into honey, making tinctures, performing bee sting treatments, etc. However, strict regulations prohibit beekeepers from labeling their products with health-promoting information. In addition, a completely new trend has emerged: apitherapy tourism. However, Italian beekeepers did not collect or use specific products made in Ukraine and Estonia, such as dead bee tincture, honeycomb moth larva tincture, and drone brood homogenates, and did not make honey moonshine. Conclusions The development of apitherapy in Europe has depended on the development of beehive types, the advancement of beekeeping technology, and new knowledge about the health-giving properties of beekeeping products (promoted in the literature and by institutions). As beekeeping is closely related to market demand, apith- erapy tourism has emerged as a completely new economic branch and apitherapy is becoming increasingly impor - tant in providing relief from mental health issues. However, this requires an entirely new approach from beekeepers and clients using apitherapy. Keywords Alternative and complementary medicine, Bee therapy, Folk remedies, Honey, Pollen, Propolis *Correspondence: Nataliya Stryamets nataliya.stryamets@slu.se Julia Prakofjewa yuliya.prakofyeva@unive.it Full list of author information is available at the end of the article Kalle et al.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the trend regarding honey production in Estonia?
nodes.answer: The trend indicates that most commercial honey will come from very large beekeeping companies in the future, with about a dozen companies already having more than 1000 hives, producing most of the honey on the market.
nodes.paragraph: The general trend, for example in Estonia, is that most commercial honey will come from very large beekeeping companies in the future. Already today, there are about a dozen companies in Estonia that have more than 1000 hives (the largest has nearly 2,0) and they produce most of the honey on the mar - ket [ 10]. A similar trend is observed in Italy, where a small percentage of professional beekeepers (3.26%) manage over 34.45% of the hives, indicating a concen - tration of production among larger operators [11]. Overview of the importance of beekeeping products and apitherapy in Europe before the period of commercialization Bees have been important to people in Europe in many ways. Honey was the only sweetener available for a long time [12]. During the Bronze Age, beeswax played an important role in various manufacturing processes, including bronze casting. Later, wax was used to make candles, especially important for churches, as well as molds and seals [8]. Another important bee product is mead (also known as honey wine), which is mentioned in Norse mythology and is still produced in the Balkans, Sweden, and elsewhere.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What factors might contribute to village hunters selling more offtake than traditional hunters?
nodes.answer: Village hunters are likely more integrated into the market economy and have better access to modern sales technologies, such as mobile phones and mobile money.
nodes.paragraph: Socio-economic variables associated with hunter offtake Our results show that the proportion of offtake sold is positively cor-related with daily hunter offtake levels. Mean daily hunter offtakes were also positively correlated with the proportion of hunters who were village hunters, as opposed to traditional forest hunter-gatherers. Village hunters typically sold a greater proportion of their offtake than traditional hunter-gatherers. These results could be because village hunters (probably including hunters coming from elsewhere specifi- cally to hunt) tend to be more integrated into the market economy than traditional forest peoples, and have better access to modern sales technologies such as mobile phones and mobile money25,38,39. Furthermore, though we acknowledge that our dataset is not longi - tudinal across the same hunters/sites, our model suggests that the proportion of animals sold has increased over time. This result could be because the demand for wild meat, particularly in urban areas, also drives the proliferation of commercial hunters and encourages some subsistence hunters to hunt for income22. These results are probably comparable to those in other parts of the tropics such as in African savannahs where wild meat is sold for income8, and in East, South and Southeast Asia40 and Latin America22 where wild meat is openly sold in markets.

nodes.question: What unique approach does this research take compared to existing studies?
nodes.answer: This research adopts a holistic approach by quantifying environmental trade-offs associated with resource exploitation and examining the interdependencies among multiple socio-economic factors.
nodes.paragraph: Second, it aims to highlight the role of education in fostering environmental consciousness and reducing ecological footprints. Additionally, the study evaluates financial inclusion S dual nature its capacity to enhance economic resilience and its potential to exacerbate environmental degradation. Lastly, the research assesses the pivotal role of technological innovation in promoting green technologies to mitigate environmental impacts. By employing advanced econometric techniques, including panel data analysis, cointegration tests, and asymmetric modeling, this study addresses gaps in empirical evidence and provides nuanced insights for policymakers. Its findings have significant implications for design- ing integrated strategies to harmonize economic growth with ecological stewardship in resource-abundant nations. This research contributes to the existing literature in several ways. First, it bridges the gap between natural resource management and sustainability studies by quantifying the environmental trade-offs associated with resource exploi- tation. While existing studies predominantly focus on individual variables, this research adopts a holistic approach, examining the interdependencies among multiple socio-economic factors. Second, the inclusion of financial inclusion and technological innovation offers a novel lens to understand their complementary roles in advancing SDGs 7 and 13.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What historical context is provided for alternative currencies in the abstract?
nodes.answer: Alternative currencies have a longer history as devices for communities aiming to reduce their dependence on the dominant economic system, predating the concept of degrowth.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract In this review, we analyze the existing literature on the role of alternative currencies within degrowth. While degrowth emerged in the early 2000s alongside growing awareness of accelerating environmental crises and widening global inequali - ties, alternative currencies have a longer history. Alternative currencies have served as devices for communities seeking to become less dependent on the dominant economic system, but degrowth and technological advancements are potentially reshaping alternative currencies, both in what their purpose could be and in how they operate. When combined with degrowth, these currencies are often expected to foster greater resilience at the local level and slow down the pace of socio-ecological metabolism. Building on our review, we propose a research agenda that explores how policy proposals and concepts such as universal basic income, localization, and entropy can be understood in relation to alternative currencies. Our main contribu- tion is to identify points of convergence and tension between alternative currencies and degrowth while proposing prospective research questions to guide future studies. Keywords Alternative currencies Complementary currencies Local currencies Social currencies Local exchange trading systems LETS Localisation Degrowth Cryptocurrencies Digital currencies Blockchain Introduction In addition to the acceleration of the environmental crisis on a global scale with consequences like climate disrup- tion, loss of biodiversity, increasing pollution, etc.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How many alternative currency systems exist, and in how many countries are they found?
nodes.answer: There are more than 5000 alternative currency systems in more than 50 countries.
nodes.paragraph: Currently, there are more than 5000 alternative cur - rency systems in more than 50 countries. The emergence of cryptocurrencies based on the block - chain technology and, especially, the creation of Bitcoin in 2009 represent landmarks in this process. One can argue that blockchain technology represents a revolution in payments like Internet was for communication 50 years ago (De Filippi 2018). Consequently, by their disruptive capacities vis- -vis banking and monetary systems, cryptocurrencies of course generate questions as to the usefulness and relevance of this technological revolution for communities and their alterna- tive currencies (Blanc 2018). Recalling the dual socio-environmental crisis, which has confronted the international community since the last cen - tury, the early 2000s saw the emergence of numerous citi- zens' movements aimed at counteracting the harmful effects of globalisation and neoliberalism. In this article, we focus on one of them: the degrowth movement. This movement was launched in France in the early 2000s by intellectuals refuting the need for economic growth. They identified and opposed economic growth as the cause of accelerating eco- logical destruction as well as widening inequalities.

nodes.question: What do global economies with high population-weighted fishing biocapacity include?
nodes.answer: Global economies with high population-weighted fishing biocapacity include the Bahamas, Suriname, Guyana, Australia, Canada, Qatar, Estonia, Norway, Guinea-Bissau, and Sweden.
